The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Strongylocentrotus pallidus reaches a value of 18% [GSI = 18%] under the frigid conditions typical of its deep-water habitat at 0 °C [T = 0 °C]. At such low temperatures, metabolic processes are substantially depressed, and the energetic investment into gamete production is correspondingly reduced relative to warmer-water congeners. These measurements underscore the constraining influence of extreme cold on the allocation of resources toward reproduction in this species.

Following external fertilisation, the zygotes of the pale sea urchin develop into free-swimming planktotrophic larvae that spend a defined period in the water column before undergoing metamorphosis. The duration of this larval phase is strongly temperature-dependent, and at a rearing temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis has been estimated at approximately 45 days . During this interval, the bipinnaria larva progresses through a series of feeding stages, grazing on phytoplankton, before developing the adult rudiment and becoming competent to settle. The 45-day pelagic period (45 days)  is a critical determinant of dispersal potential, as longer larval durations increase the likelihood of transport to distant substrates at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This value is comparable to that reported for the closely related Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis under similar thermal conditions, suggesting a conserved developmental schedule within the genus at cold temperatures.

The lifespan of Strongylocentrotus pallidus is remarkably extended, a trait that reflects the profoundly low metabolic rates imposed by its cold-water environment. Field studies and laboratory maintenance at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] have indicated a maximum longevity of approximately 42 years [am = approximately 42 years], a duration that places this species among the longer-lived echinoids. This extreme lifespan likely arises from a combination of slow somatic growth, delayed sexual maturation, and reduced predation pressure in deep, cold habitats. The 42-year maximum (42 years) [am = 42 years] represents a stark contrast to short-lived tropical sea urchins, which often complete their entire life cycle in just a few years at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. Energetically, a prolonged lifespan permits multiple reproductive events across many seasons, allowing individuals to buffer against sporadic recruitment failures and to allocate resources gradually toward both maintenance and gamete production over decades rather than concentrating effort into a single brief reproductive window.

Estimates of the test diameter at which this species attains reproductive maturity have been derived from comparative data on the congener Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis, given the morphological and ecological similarities between the two taxa. For S. pallidus, the test diameter at puberty is approximately 2.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 2.5 centimeters], a size that corresponds to several years of slow post-metamorphic growth under natural thermal conditions. This pubertal size is modest relative to the ultimate test diameter of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters] that the species can achieve over its extended lifespan. The gap between the size at maturity (2.5 cm [Lp = 2.5 cm]) and the asymptotic size (9 cm [Li = 9 cm]) indicates a prolonged adult growth phase during which individuals continue to increase in body size while simultaneously allocating energy to annual reproductive cycles. Such a pattern is typical of indeterminate growers that inhabit stable, resource-limited environments where incremental gains in body volume confer advantages in fecundity and competitive ability over many decades.

The initial wet weight of the newly fertilised ovum in Strongylocentrotus pallidus is exceptionally small, reflecting the typical echinoderm pattern of broadcasting numerous tiny gametes into the water column. Based on an assumed egg diameter of 130 micrometers, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 1.15 × 10⁻⁶ grams [Wwb = approximately 1.15 × 10⁻⁶ grams]. This minuscule starting mass represents the entire maternal investment per offspring, as there is no additional parental care following broadcast fertilisation. The planktotrophic larva must therefore obtain virtually all of its subsequent growth from exogenous feeding during its 45-day larval period (45 days)  in the plankton at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The low Wwb (1.15 × 10⁻⁶ grams) [Wwb = 1.15 × 10⁻⁶ grams] value, when contrasted with the ultimate adult test diameter of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters] and the 42-year (42 years [am = 42 years]) lifespan, illustrates the extraordinary scope of ontogenetic growth achieved by this species across its long life, despite the energetic constraints imposed by its persistently cold environment at 7 °C [T = 7 °C].
